entries.title: Acts 21:1
segments:
Cos. A small island near the coast of Asia Minor.
 

 
Rhodes. A large island lying south of Caria.  Its capital city was of the same name, and was celebrated for its great Temple of the Sun, and the Colossus, the famous statue at the entrance to the harbor.  The latter was one hundred and five feet high, and was a representation of the Sun god.
 

 
Patara. A city on the coast of Lycia.

entries.title: Acts 21:3
segments: Cyprus. See notes on

.
 

 
Tyre. The greatest of maritime cities in ancient times.  Its fleets of merchant ships once far exceeded those of any other nation.  It was famed for its manufacture of purple dye and glass.  Its sailors were capable and daring, and its trade was carried to and from all the countries of the civilized world.  In Paul's time it had lost much of its ancient glory, thought it was still important.

entries.title: Acts 21:5
segments: Accomplished the days. The seven days of their stay at Tyre.

segments: Who prophesied. That is, preached the gospel, as did their father.  The word 'prophesy' has only comparatively recently been restricted in meaning to 'predict,' in the sense of foretelling the future.

entries.title: Acts 21:26
segments: Paul took the men, etc.  He did this in accordance with the recommendation of James and the elders, in order to show that he was a good Jew in keeping the law, and to ward off controversial discord over the question of his advising his Gentile converts to ignore the Jewish customs.

entries.title: Acts 21:27
segments: The Jews from Asia. That is, those who had known or heard of him during his missionary labors in the province of Asia.

entries.title: Acts 21:31
segments: The chief captain of the band. The commander of the Roman garrison in the fortress of Antonia.

entries.title: Acts 21:32
segments: Left off beating Paul. A beneficent interference that probably saved the apostle's life.

entries.title: Acts 21:38
segments:
The Egyptian. One of the imposters and rebels of that time.
 

 
The Assassins. Or the Sicarii.  Men armed with daggers, who mixed with crowds, wounded some by stabbing them, and then pretended to join in the hunt for the guilty ones.  In this way they often evaded arrest.
